To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) taste receptor cell death is mediated by p53 and BAX, (2) p53 is present in post‐mitotic, aged receptor cells, and (3) the expression of p53 and BAG by aged receptor cells excludes some explanations for the stability of taste signals.
p53 and BAX are putative death factors in the turnover of taste receptor cells.
p53 and BAX are present in aged taste receptor cells in mouse lingual epithelia, and that the presence of these putative death factors is associated with death of the taste cells.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the turnover of taste receptor cells.
the turnover of cells in a renewing epithelium, the tongue.
the turnover of taste receptor cells, and with the role of p53 and BAX in taste cell death.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
p53 and BAX are not involved in normal taste cell turnover.
p53 and BAX are involved in the turnover of taste cells.
p53 and BAX are putative death factors in the turnover of taste receptor cells.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the p53 and Bcl‐2 families of death factors are expressed in taste receptor cells, but only in aged receptor cells.
taste receptor cells die by apoptosis.
p53 and BAX are expressed in a subset of aged, nonproliferating taste receptor cells.
The main takeaway from our work is that
taste receptor cells die in an orderly way that involves the expression of p53 and BAX.
taste receptor cells are not the only cells in the taste bud that die, as had been previously assumed.
p53 and BAX are not expressed in taste receptor cells until they are about 5 days old, which is when they start to die.
